Example: 
                    Stating the Definition of Integer Divisibility
problem:
Fill in the blanks so that the following reasoning is correct:

The notation $3 \mid 18$ means ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14114596/assets/06b772f72fe6d6f1ee02bdc961f6438561083573e0e0d9d261c7594cd48e86bc.svg) It is equivalent to the statement that there exists 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14114596/assets/c4ebc4da7c8037d0ca6a752df8a4dc3933918db39ac972e4a9b5068fac834140.svg) such that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14114596/assets/88e94f9f45ba18035aaea40fb665ecd374c878f9ac7c44aeb038f2d210c02a28.svg)
worked_solution:
The notation $a \mid b$ means $a$ divides $b.$ So, $3 \mid 18$ means ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14114596/assets/5aaf3d46d0bf568ead42806495080fa6eab9d567aa33d22faeee925233867b0a.svg)

According to the definition of integer divisibility, the fact that $a$ divides $b$ means that there exists an integer $k$ such that 

$$
b=a k.
$$

 

Therefore, $3 \mid 18$ is equivalent to the statement that there exists $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\textrm{an integer}}$ $k$ such that $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}18 = 3k}.$
